claims.text: Enhancing local chemical order in a multi-component concentrated alloy increases its strength.
Enhancing local chemical order alters the alloy's deformation behavior.
Local chemical order induces spatial fluctuations in local shear-fault or stacking-fault energies.
Fault-energy fluctuations associated with local chemical order create additional dislocation-pinning sites.
A cast and high-temperature-homogenized equiatomic CrCoNi or NiCoCr single-phase solid solution has a nearly random atomic distribution with minimal local chemical order.
A controlled lower-temperature anneal or thermomechanical treatment can increase local chemical order relative to the baseline.
Enhanced local chemical order forms localized ordered regions described as hard atomic motifs.
Localized ordered regions produce pronounced spatial fluctuations in the alloy's fault-energy landscape.
Regions with greater local chemical order have higher local shear-fault or stacking-fault energies.
Dislocations are pinned as they move through the proposed high-fault-energy hard zones.
Pinning at locally ordered hard zones increases the activation barrier for dislocation glide.
The increased barrier to dislocation glide raises yield strength.
The proposed pinning mechanism typically increases strain hardening.
The proposed increase in strain hardening delays deformation localization and failure.
At room temperature and otherwise identical test conditions, the LCO-enhanced sample will have greater yield strength than the random-solution baseline.
At room temperature and otherwise identical test conditions, the LCO-enhanced sample will have a higher strain-hardening rate than the random-solution baseline.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for single-phase, equiatomic multi-component concentrated alloys under room-temperature tensile loading at comparable strain rates.
Changes in phase stability or processing conditions may alter the proposed relationship.
